item.title: Introduction to Multilevel Modeling — Wed Sep 9, 9:00 AM
item.description:
This course will take place over two days (9/9/2026 and 9/11/2026) and will be offered via Zoom. Attendance is required as the course will not be recorded.
Nesting can arise from hierarchical data structures (e.g., siblings nested within family; patients nested within therapist), longitudinal data structures (repeated measures nested within individual), or both (repeated measures nested within patient and patient nested within therapist).
It is well known that the analysis of nested data structures using traditional general linear models (e.g., ANOVA or regression) is flawed, oftentimes substantially so: Tests of significance are likely biased and within- and between-group effects are confounded with one another. All of these limitations can be addressed within the multilevel model.
In this workshop, we provide an introduction to the application of multilevel models with nested data, including software implementation in SAS, SPSS and Stata.

item.title: DQC Seminar Series: Nuclear clocks: What next? — Thu Sep 10, 12:00 PM — None
item.description: In 1976 Kroger and Reich established the existence of a low-lying nuclear excited state in 229Th through the spectroscopy of γ rays emitted following the α decay of 233U. The prospects of a laser-accessible nuclear transition touched off a flurry of proposals to utilize this apparently unique nuclear transition as a sensitive probe of both nuclear structure and chemical environment, to constrain physics beyond the Standard Model, and to construct a clock with unprecedented performance. Unfortunately, Kroger and Reich could only tell us that the transition energy was less than about 100 eV and therefore scientists have spent the intervening 48 years searching for the thorium nuclear transition. In 2024, there was a breakthrough in this search and the nuclear transition was finally laser excited in Th:CaF2 [1,2] at PTB and JILA, and in Th:LiSrAlF6 [3], ThF4 [4], and ThO2 [5] at UCLA. item.title: Not All Shift Work Is Equal: Disentangling Schedule Type and Night-Work Exposure in Cognitive Aging in Older Latinos — Thu Sep 10, 12:00 PM — SSRI-Gross Hall 270
item.description: Work shapes not only economic security but long-term health, including the trajectory of cognitive aging. For Latino adults-who face elevated risk for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias and are disproportionately concentrated in service, manufacturing, and construction jobs with limited schedule control-occupational exposures may be an underrecognized driver of this disparity. Shift work, in particular, may compound risk through chronic circadian disruption, yet its cognitive consequences remain unexamined in this population. We introduce a novel application of longitudinal data from the Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos and its neurocognitive aging ancillary study, using a detailed shift-work index that captures both schedule type and night-work frequency to assess cognitive function and change over roughly seven years among adults employed at baseline. We find that regular night-shift work is associated with persistently lower processing speed and verbal fluency

item.title: Screening: Her Fight, His Name: The Story of Gwen Carr and Eric Garner — Thu Sep 10, 12:00 PM — Smith Warehouse
item.description:
"Her Fight, His Name: The Story of Gwen Carr and Eric Garner" (Brad Bailey, 2024, 30m) Discussion to follow with Director Brad Bailey and Mrs. Gwen Carr.
The short documentary centers on Gwen Carr's enduring fight for justice following the 2014 death of her son, Eric Garner, after being pinned to the ground in a chokehold by a police officer in Staten Island. The New York City medical examiner stated the cause of death as a homicide. Garner's final words, "I can't breathe," became a rallying cry in protests against police violence and systemic racism across the United States. Filmed over several years, the documentary places Carr's voice at its core, tracing her transformation from grieving mother to nationally recognized advocate for accountability and human rights.
Winner of the 2026 Human Rights Digital Storytelling Award sponsored by the David M. Rubenstein Rare book and Manuscript Library.

Terrie Moffitt, PhD, a licensed clinical psychologist, is the Nannerl O. Keohane University Professor of Psychology at Duke University and professor of social development at King's College London. Her expertise is in longitudinal methods, developmental theory, mental disorders and antisocial behaviors, neuropsychology, and genomics in behavioral science.

item.title: A Poetic Politics of Shade in Saigon — Thu Sep 10, 3:00 PM — Rubenstein Library Carpenter Conference Room 249
item.description:
The congenial pockets of shade cast by Ho Chi Minh City's tamarind trees, dipterocarps, and African mahoganies are, in some very literal ways, colonial shadows. Many of the trees were planted directly by the French, and trees planted by successive regimes also followed the model of those earliest French treescapes. While there is much to cherish about Saigon's trees, they were rooted in a larger colonial discourse through which the French simultaneously justified colonial rule and denigrated indigenous Vietnamese modes of habitation.
Similar dynamics can also be found in post-war and post-reform Ho Chi Minh City. Like the French, contemporary government and city leaders also assert their legitimacy through urban tree planting programs, even as they routinely ignore local experience and knowledge by felling trees to make way for infrastructure projects. item.description:
Join the Center for Jewish Studies Fall 2026 welcome reception which will also celebrate the recent publications of Duke faculty members Kata Gellen and Daniel Herskowitz. Dinner will be provided.
Kata Gellen, Galicia as a Literary Idea: Jewish Eastern Europe in the Writings of Joseph Roth and Soma Morgenstern. (University of Toronto Press, 2026). In the decades following the dissolution of Austria-Hungary, the former province of Galicia inspired the literary imagination of two German-language natives of this region, Joseph Roth and Soma Morgenstern. Galicia as a Literary Idea explores what their engagement with Galicia means for modern Jewish culture, history, and memory.
Gellen is Associate Professor of German Studies and Director of the Center for Jewish Studies. item.title: Introduction to Multilevel Modeling — Fri Sep 11, 9:00 AM
item.description:
This course will take place over two days (9/9/2026 and 9/11/2026) and will be offered via Zoom. Attendance is required as the course will not be recorded.
Nesting can arise from hierarchical data structures (e.g., siblings nested within family; patients nested within therapist), longitudinal data structures (repeated measures nested within individual), or both (repeated measures nested within patient and patient nested within therapist).
It is well known that the analysis of nested data structures using traditional general linear models (e.g., ANOVA or regression) is flawed, oftentimes substantially so: Tests of significance are likely biased and within- and between-group effects are confounded with one another. All of these limitations can be addressed within the multilevel model.
In this workshop, we provide an introduction to the application of multilevel models with nested data, including software implementation in SAS, SPSS and Stata.

item.title: Lectures in Art History: Art, Health, and Equity series featuring Tanya Sheehan, Colby College — Mon Sep 14, 5:30 PM — Chapman Hall
item.description:
Department of Art and Art History
“Communities of Care: Charles Alston, Jacob Lawrence, and the Murals of Harlem Hospital”
When Jacob Lawrence first painted an image of Harlem Hospital in 1937, Harlem’s largest public healthcare facility was teamed with artists hired by the federal government and working under the supervision of Lawrence’s art teacher and mentor, Charles Alston. Although the young painter was not officially assigned to Alston’s team, significant connections to the murals can be found in his artwork, in the murals themselves, and in their shared participation in a discourse on race, medicine, and health in urban America. In exploring these connections, this talk shows how Black life could and could not be represented on the walls of Harlem Hospital, and how a commitment to care within and for Black communities took shape in Lawrence’s art.
Tanya Sheehan is James M. Gillespie Professor and Chair of the Department of Science, Technology, and Society at Colby

Come by for a few minutes or stay for the full session to ask questions, explore tools, solve problems and make meaningful progress toward expanding access.
Progress Over Perfection
Progress means recognizing common barriers in the platforms you use and taking small steps to reduce them. It’s choosing web formats over PDFs, applying table headers, checking color contrast and collaborating on accessible templates so everyone can start from a strong foundation. item.description:

item.title: Designing AI-Assisted Qualitative Research Workflows — Thu Sep 17, 9:00 AM
item.description:
This one-day course will be offered via Zoom only. Attendance is required as it will not be recorded.
This interactive, hands-on workshop will introduce participants to a framework for considering the consequences of using generative AI in qualitative research designs and workflows (Paulus, 2023; Paulus & Lester, 2024). We will start by acknowledging inherent risks and ethical dilemmas posed by the development of large language models and how generative AI is challenging the essence of what it means to do qualitative work (Paulus & Marone, 2025; Paulus, Lester & Davis, 2025). We will learn how to distinguish between methodological strategies and technological tactics, i.e. why researchers must first know how they want to work with their data before choosing the best tools to do so (Woolf & Silver, 2018). item.title: Healthy AI Use: Avoiding an Echo Chamber — Thu Sep 17, 9:00 AM — 79 Degrees West
item.description:
An AI affirms your position ~49% more than a person would, and even one agreeable exchange hardens your conviction that you're right. Early research suggests that even when we become aware of this, it doesn't reduce how influential our AI can be. We inherently trust AI (and people) that flatter us, and this module goes deeper into what that leads to, how to audit it happening, and where you can rebuild boundaries or rules for healthy, structured habits.
Source: UNC Chapel Hill

item.description:
We all have a role to play in promoting mental health and preventing suicide. Whether you're a parent, coach, faith leader, educator, healthcare professional, coworker, friend, or neighbor, the right knowledge and tools can help you recognize when someone may be struggling, offer support, and connect them to resources.
The Path to Prevention is a community-centered summit and training event designed for individuals who want to build a stronger foundation in mental health and suicide prevention. Whether you're new to these topics or looking to better understand how to recognize concerns and connect others with support, this event will provide practical, accessible knowledge and resources.

item.title: Pursuing Funding in the Public and Private Sectors: Opportunities and Challenges — Fri Sep 18, 9:00 AM
item.description:
Securing funding is one of the most consequential — and least openly discussed — dimensions of a research career. For scholars whose work centers social inequality and structurally marginalized communities, pursuing funding carries unique political and institutional complexities. This workshop engages those realities directly. Participants will examine how funding priorities are shaped, how research agendas can be both advanced and constrained by funders, and how to build a diversified, sustainable funding strategy across sectors — without losing sight of their scholarly mission or community commitments.
In this workshop, Dr. Rashawn Ray, whose funding portfolio spans federal agencies, private foundations, and philanthropic institutions, will demystify the landscape of public and private research support.
